subject: Business
title: Open Innovation: Ideas From Everywhere
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Open Innovation: Ideas From Everywhere.

hook.text: Procter & Gamble's 'Connect + Develop' program sources 50% of innovations from outside the company.

buildup.text: Open innovation means using external ideas, technologies, and partnerships alongside internal R&D.

discovery.text: Henry Chesbrough argued that useful knowledge is widely distributed. No company can monopolize all smart people.

twist.text: The 'not invented here' syndrome causes companies to reject external ideas. Pride blocks better solutions.

climax.text: Linux, Wikipedia, and Android all prove that open, collaborative innovation can outperform closed corporate R&D.

punchline.text: The best ideas don't care where they were born.

quiz.question: What is the core principle of open innovation?
options: Useful ideas can come from outside the company and should be embraced
Only internal R&D can produce valuable innovations
Sharing all company secrets with competitors

details.summary: Open innovation uses external ideas, technologies, and partnerships alongside internal R&D to accelerate innovation. Coined by Henry Chesbrough, it recognizes that the most useful knowledge often resides outside a company's walls and must be systematically accessed.
details.whyItMatters: No company can hire all the smart people. Open innovation taps the global talent pool through partnerships, acquisitions, licensing, and crowdsourcing, dramatically expanding innovative capacity beyond internal resources alone.
takeaways: Open innovation accesses external ideas alongside internal research efforts
Partnerships, licensing, and acquisitions bring outside knowledge inside
Procter & Gamble's Connect + Develop sources over half its innovations externally

faq.question: What is a real-world example of open innovation succeeding?
faq.answer: Procter & Gamble's Connect + Develop program sources innovations from external networks. Over half of P&G's product innovations involve external partners. This approach helped develop Swiffer, Crest Whitestrips, and Febreze by combining internal capabilities with outside inventions.

faq.question: What are the risks of open innovation?
faq.answer: Intellectual property leakage when sharing with partners, dependence on external sources for critical innovations, coordination costs across organizational boundaries, and the not-invented-here bias where internal teams resist external ideas. Strong IP agreements and cultural change are essential.
